content.alt_text: A horizontal bench labelled 'Bench' stands on a single vertical leg on a horizontal line labelled 'Floor'. A small shaded ball rests on the top of the bench with a horizontal arrow to the right showing its velocity, and a dashed parabolic path curves from the ball down to the floor on the right.

content.text: Rolling the marble at a slower speed would
increase the range.
decrease the range.
increase the time of flight.
decrease the time of flight.
The marble leaves the bench horizontally, so work out how long it is in the air first: that depends only on the height of the bench above the floor, not on how fast it is rolling.
Then relate the horizontal distance it covers to that flight time and its horizontal speed.
B
h = \frac{1}{2}gt^2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}
The marble leaves the bench horizontally, so it has no initial vertical velocity and the fall time depends only on the height $h$ of the bench. Rolling it faster or slower does not change that time.

The horizontal range is $x = v_x t$. With $t$ fixed, a smaller horizontal speed gives a smaller range, so the range decreases and the time of flight is unchanged. That rules out both time options, leaving B, decrease the range.

items: 1 mark: selects B, recognising that the time of flight is set by the height of the bench alone and the horizontal range is $x = v_{x}t$, so a lower launch speed gives a smaller range

content.text: What is the direction of the force acting on the particle due to the electric field?
Into the page
Out of the page
Up the page
Down the page

Use $F = qE$ and keep track of the sign of the charge. The parallel arrows on the diagram give the direction of the electric field, and the force on a positive charge is along the field while the force on a negative charge is against it.
C

The electric field is uniform and directed upwards, along the parallel arrows. The force on a charge in a uniform electric field is $F = qE$, so for a positive charge the force is in the same direction as the field.

The particle is positively charged, so the force on it is up the page, in the direction of the field arrows. Its velocity is horizontal, so it accelerates upwards and follows a curved path. The correct option is C.

items: 1 mark: selects C, applying the convention that a positive charge experiences a force in the direction of the electric field (up the page, from the positive to the negative plate)

content.text: Which of the following is NOT a fundamental particle in the Standard Model of matter?
Electron
Gluon
Muon
Proton

The Standard Model treats matter as six quarks and six leptons, together with the bosons that carry the forces. Work through the options asking which one is built out of those building blocks rather than being one of them.
A useful test: if a particle can be broken up into a group of quarks, it is a composite particle and is not fundamental.
D

The electron and the muon are both leptons: point-like fundamental particles with no known substructure, and both are part of the Standard Model. The gluon is the gauge boson that carries the strong nuclear force between quarks, so it too is a fundamental particle.
The proton is different. It is a baryon made from three valence quarks bound by the strong force, so its charge arises from the combination of those quark charges:
Because it is a composite of three quarks, the proton is the option that is not a fundamental particle of matter, which is D.

items: 1 mark: selects D, recognising that the electron, muon and gluon are fundamental particles whereas the proton is a baryon composed of three quarks

content.text: An astronaut is travelling towards Earth in a spaceship at $0.8c$. At regular intervals, a radio pulse is sent from the spaceship to an observer on Earth.
Which quantity would the astronaut and the observer measure to be the same?
Length of the spaceship
Speed of the radio pulses
Momentum of the astronaut
Time interval between the radio pulses
Einstein's first postulate says the speed of light in a vacuum has the same value for every inertial observer, however the source and observer are moving.
Check the other three quantities at $v = 0.8c$ using $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1-v^{2}/c^{2}} = 1.67$: each of them is frame-dependent.
B
Length: the astronaut measures the ship to be Lorentz contracted, $l = l_0/\gamma = 0.60\,l_0$, while the Earth observer measures $l_0$.
Momentum: $p = \gamma m_0 v$ depends on the frame, so the two observers measure different momenta.
Time interval between pulses: $\Delta t = \gamma \Delta t_0$, so the Earth observer measures the pulses arriving further apart (time dilation).

Speed of the radio pulses: light travels at $c$ in a vacuum in every inertial frame, so both observers measure $3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. This is the only quantity they agree on, so the answer is B.

items: 1 mark: selects B, recognising that all observers measure the same speed $c$ for electromagnetic radiation in a vacuum, while the other quantities are frame-dependent (length contraction, relativistic momentum, time dilation)

content.alt_text: Graph of an object's spectrum. Vertical axis 'Intensity' (unnumbered), horizontal axis 'Wavelength (nm)' from 350 to 700 in steps of 50. content.text: Which row of the table correctly identifies the most likely source of the spectrum and the features labelled $Y$?
Star: Absorption lines
Discharge tube: Absorption lines
Star: Emission lines
Discharge tube: Emission lines
Decide first what kind of spectrum the trace shows: a continuous band covering all wavelengths, bright lines on a dark background, or a continuous band with dark lines cut into it.
The arrows labelled $Y$ point to dips in the trace, so they mark wavelengths at which less light reaches the detector than in the surrounding continuum.
A

The trace is a broad continuous band, so the source radiates at all these wavelengths. A hot, dense body such as a star produces such a spectrum; a low-pressure discharge tube does not, because a dilute gas emits only discrete wavelengths and appears as bright lines on a dark background.

The features labelled $Y$ are sharp downward lines, i.e. wavelengths at which less light is detected than in the surrounding continuum. Those are absorption lines: cooler material in the outer layers of the source absorbs exactly the wavelengths its atoms can absorb, cutting dark lines into an otherwise continuous spectrum.
Only the row 'Star / Absorption lines' is consistent with the trace, which is option A.

items: 1 mark: selects A, identifying the spectrum as that of a star (a hot continuous source) and recognising that the dark features labelled $Y$ are absorption lines

content.text: The diagram shows part of a nuclear fusion process that occurs in stars.

content.alt_text: Diagram of part of a nuclear fusion process. Two protons (dotted circles) converge on a star-shaped reaction point, from which a neutrino v and a positron (open circle) emerge and a deuterium nucleus (one proton plus one dark cross-hatched neutron) travels to the right. That nucleus meets a further proton at a second star-shaped point, from which a gamma ray gamma is emitted and a nucleus of three particles labelled R is produced. A key box on the right lists: Proton (dotted circle), Neutron (dark cross-hatched circle), Positron (open circle), Gamma ray (gamma), Neutrino (v).

content.text: What is the isotope labelled $R$ ?
He-2
He-3
Apply conservation of mass number (total nucleon count) and conservation of charge (proton count) to the second stage shown in the diagram.
Remember that a gamma ray carries away energy but no charge and no nucleons, and that the positron emitted in the first stage removed one proton's worth of charge.
D

First stage: two protons ($A = 2$, $Z = 2$) produce a positron (charge $+1$), a neutrino (no charge) and a deuterium nucleus, so the deuterium nucleus must contain one proton and one neutron ($A = 2$, $Z = 1$).
Second stage: that deuterium nucleus fuses with an incoming proton to produce $R$ and a gamma ray.
The gamma ray carries off energy but contributes nothing to either total, so $R$ has mass number 3 and atomic number 2. It is helium-3, ${}^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He}$, which is option D.
The other rows fail: H-2 and H-3 have only one proton ($Z = 1$), and He-2 has mass number 2.

items: 1 mark: selects D, conserving mass number ($2 + 1 = 3$) and atomic number ($1 + 1 = 2$) to identify $R$ as He-3

content.text: In a certain ideal transformer, the current in the secondary coil is four times as large as the current in the primary coil.
Which row of the table correctly identifies the type of transformer and the ratio of turns?
Step up: $4 : 1$
Step up: $1 : 4$
Step down: $4 : 1$
Step down: $1 : 4$
For an ideal transformer the input power equals the output power: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$. Use $I_s = 4 I_p$ to work out what $V_s$ must be.
Then connect that to the turns ratio with $V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s$, remembering that a step-down transformer has more turns in the primary than in the secondary.
C

content.latex: V_p I_p = V_s I_s \;\Rightarrow\; V_s = \frac{V_p I_p}{I_s} = \frac{V_p I_p}{4 I_p} = \frac{V_p}{4}

content.text: The secondary voltage is one quarter of the primary voltage, so this is a step-down transformer.

A step-down transformer with four times as many primary turns as secondary turns is row C. Rows A and B are self-contradictory, because a step-up transformer must have more turns in the secondary, and row D has the turns ratio the wrong way round for a step-down transformer.

items: 1 mark: selects C, using $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$ with $I_s = 4 I_p$ to deduce the secondary voltage (and hence number of turns) is lower than the primary, so the transformer is a step-down with $N_p : N_s = 4 : 1$

content.text: Light from a point source is incident upon a circular metal disc, forming a shadow on a screen as shown. A bright spot is observed in the centre of the shadow.

content.alt_text: Perspective view of an optical set-up on a bench. A 'Point source of light' on the left shines on a small circular 'Metal disc' mounted on a stand. Beyond it a vertical screen carries a shadow with a bright spot at its centre; leader lines label the illuminated centre 'Bright spot' and the plate 'Screen'.

content.text: The bright spot is caused by a combination of
interference and refraction.
refraction and polarisation.
polarisation and diffraction.
diffraction and interference.
This is the same effect that puts a small bright spot at the centre of the shadow of someone's hair on a sunny day. A bright spot in the middle of a shadow can only be explained by wave behaviour.

Light passing the edge of the disc is bent around it. At the point directly behind the centre of the disc, light from every part of that bent wavefront has travelled the same distance, so what happens when those waves arrive together?
D

Light passing a circular edge is diffracted, so the wavefronts bend around the disc and the geometric shadow is not perfectly dark. At the point on the axis directly behind the centre of the disc, light has travelled an equal distance from every point on the rim, so the diffracted waves arrive in phase.

These waves therefore interfere constructively at that point and reinforce one another, producing the bright Poisson (Arago) spot at the centre of the shadow. The bright spot is caused by a combination of diffraction and interference, which is option D.

Refraction is the bending of light caused by a change of speed on entering a new medium, which plays no part here, and polarisation concerns the orientation of the electric field, which is not what produces the spot.

items: 1 mark: selects D, recognising that light diffracts around the circular disc (Poisson/Arago spot) and the diffracted waves from opposite edges interfere constructively on the axis to produce the bright spot

content.text: Which graph best represents the gravitational potential energy, $U$, of the mass during this movement?

content.alt_text: Graph with vertical axis U and horizontal axis Time. The plotted line is horizontal throughout, at a constant non-zero positive value of U, so U does not change with time.

content.text: Write the potential energy of the mass as $U = -2GMm/r$ and ask what happens to $r$, the distance from the mass to each star, as it moves from the midpoint out to $X$.

Since $U$ is negative, think about what increasing $r$ does to its magnitude, and note that the gravitational field weakens with distance so the rate of change of $U$ must fall off as the mass recedes.
C
At the midpoint $M$ the distance to each star is $d$, half the separation between them. At $X$ the mass has moved perpendicular to the line of centres, so $r = \sqrt{d^{2} + y^{2}} > d$.

Because $U$ is negative, increasing $r$ makes $U$ less negative, so $U$ increases towards zero as the mass recedes from the stars, and it increases at a decreasing rate because the field weakens with distance.
The official answer is option C: it is the only graph whose final value lies above its starting value and whose gradient decreases as the mass moves away.

content.alt_text: A large shaded rectangular block drawn in perspective. A bar magnet stands vertically in front of its front face, with N at the top and S at the bottom, and a horizontal arrow labelled v points to the right showing the magnet's direction of motion past the block. content.text: What is the direction of the force acting on the copper block?
To the left
To the right
Into the page
Out of the page
Eddy currents are induced in the copper whenever the magnetic flux through it changes. Decide whether those induced currents help the magnet along or oppose it.
Lenz's law states that the induced effect always opposes the change that produced it, so it is always a braking effect.
B

As the magnet approaches the copper, the flux through the block increases. The induced eddy currents flow so as to oppose that increase, making the face of the block nearest the magnet behave like a pole that repels it.

As the magnet moves away, the induced currents hold the block back, opposing the separation. In both stages the magnetic force on the block acts in the same direction as the magnet's velocity, dragging the block to the right.

This is the principle of electromagnetic braking, and the force must oppose the relative motion: a force assisting it would create energy. A force to the left, or into or out of the page, cannot be correct, so the answer is B.

items: 1 mark: selects B, applying Lenz's law: as the magnet approaches, eddy currents are induced in the copper that oppose the increase in flux, and the resulting magnetic interaction opposes the relative motion (drags the block to the right)

content.text: What is the peak wavelength of electromagnetic radiation emitted by a person with a body temperature of $37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ($310\,\mathrm{K}$)?
$9.3 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}$
$7.8 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}$
$9.3 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$

Use Wien's displacement law $\lambda_{max} = b/T$ with $b = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m\,K}$.
Check your working dimensionally: with $b$ in $\mathrm{m\,K}$ and $T$ in kelvin the result is a length in metres, so make sure you divide by the temperature rather than multiply by it.
A
The peak wavelength lies in the infrared region, as expected for a body at body temperature.

The value $7.8 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}$ is obtained by dividing by 37 instead of 310, that is by using the Celsius temperature where kelvin is required; the other values come from mishandling the powers of ten. The correct peak wavelength is $9.3 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}$, which is option A.

content.text: Which graph shows the magnitude of back emf induced in a DC motor rotating continuously at different angular velocities?

content.alt_text: Graph with vertical axis 'Magnitude of back emf' and horizontal axis 'Angular velocity'. A curve rises from the origin with increasing gradient, convex upwards throughout, so the back emf increases faster than linearly with angular velocity.

Graph with vertical axis 'Magnitude of back emf' and horizontal axis 'Angular velocity'. A straight line of negative gradient falls from a positive value at zero angular velocity to zero at the right-hand end of the axis.

Graph with vertical axis 'Magnitude of back emf' and horizontal axis 'Angular velocity'. The curve rises steeply from the origin, then bends over and flattens, approaching a maximum at the right-hand end; the gradient decreases with increasing angular velocity.
Graph with vertical axis 'Magnitude of back emf' and horizontal axis 'Angular velocity'. A single straight line of constant positive gradient passes through the origin from bottom left to top right.

content.text: The back emf is produced by the coil of the motor itself cutting the magnetic flux as it rotates, so use $|\varepsilon| = NBA\sin\theta$ with the coil at the angle of maximum flux cutting. What is $\sin\theta$ at that instant?

Also consider the value of the emf at zero angular velocity: nothing cuts the flux when the motor is stationary, so the graph must pass through the origin. Then decide whether the relationship is a straight line or a curve.
D

The emf is largest when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, so the magnitude of the back emf is directly proportional to the angular velocity, $|\varepsilon_{back}| = k\omega$ where $k = NBA$ for that coil.

The graph is therefore a straight line of constant positive gradient through the origin, since no flux is cut at all when the motor is at rest. That is option D. Option A wrongly suggests a quadratic relationship, option C suggests the emf saturates, and option B has the wrong gradient and a non-zero intercept.

items: 1 mark: selects the correct graph, recognising that the back emf in a DC motor is generated by the rotating coil so it is zero at rest and increases directly in proportion to angular velocity, $\varepsilon_{back} \propto \omega$

content.text: Which of the following statements correctly describes the gravitational interaction between the Earth and the Moon?
The Earth accelerates towards the Moon.
The net force acting on the Earth is zero.
The Moon and Earth experience equal and opposite accelerations.
The force acting on the Moon is smaller than the force acting on the Earth.
The gravitational forces the two bodies exert on each other form an action-reaction pair, so they must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Now apply $a = F/m$ to each body in turn.
The Earth's mass is many times greater than the Moon's, so the same force produces a much smaller acceleration on the Earth.
A

By Newton's law of universal gravitation the Earth pulls on the Moon and the Moon pulls on the Earth with forces of equal magnitude. That eliminates B, C and D: the net force on the Earth is not zero, the accelerations are not equal, and the forces on the two bodies are equal rather than smaller for the Moon.
The Earth's acceleration is about 81 times smaller than the Moon's because of its much greater mass, but it is not zero. The Earth does accelerate towards the Moon, so option A is correct.

items: 1 mark: selects A, recognising that the gravitational forces on the Earth and Moon are equal and opposite but the Earth's far greater mass means its acceleration is much smaller, so it does accelerate towards the Moon

content.text: How would $I_1$ and $I_2$ be affected if the transmission axis of the first polariser was rotated?
Both would change.
Only $I_1$ would change.
Only $I_2$ would change.

An ideal polariser always transmits exactly half the intensity of unpolarised light, whatever the orientation of its transmission axis, so first ask whether $I_1$ depends on that orientation at all.

The second polariser is fixed, so rotating the first changes the angle $\theta$ between the two axes and therefore changes $\cos^{2}\theta$, and with it $I_2$. Hence only $I_2$ changes and option C is correct. If neither changed, the second polariser would have no effect at all, which is not the purpose of the arrangement.

content.text: Which statement correctly compares the forces measured by the spring balances?
The forces measured on $X$ and $Y$ will always be equal.
The force measured on $Y$ will be greater than or equal to that on $X$.
The force measured on $X$ will be greater than or equal to that on $Y$.
There will be a continuous reversal of which measured force is greater.
First decide the direction of the current in each conductor as the single circuit circulates, then recall whether parallel currents flowing in the same direction attract or repel.

Remember that each spring balance reads the tension needed to hold its conductor up, which combines the conductor's weight with the magnetic force on it. Ask which way the magnetic force pushes each conductor.
C

The circuit is a single loop, so the current travels along $Y$ from left to right and returns along $X$ from right to left. The currents in the two conductors are anti-parallel, so the conductors repel.

The repulsive force pushes $X$ downwards and $Y$ upwards, so the balances supporting $X$ read $W + F_{mag}$ while those supporting $Y$ read $W - F_{mag}$. With identical conductors the weights are the same, so the measured force on $X$ is always greater than that on $Y$.

The phrase 'greater than or equal to' in the correct option covers the instants in each AC cycle when the current, and hence $F_{mag}$, passes through zero and both sets of balances read only the bare weight. The measured forces are never equal at the same instant and their order is never reversed, so option C is correct.

The readings are never equal at the same instant and their order is never reversed.

The long plate is connected to the positive terminal of the cell, so the electric field between the plates points horizontally, from the long positive plate towards the short negative plate. The field is horizontal, not vertical.

content.text: A student measures the current, $I$, when the power supply is set to zero. They then measure the stopping voltage, $V_s$. The stopping voltage is the minimum voltage needed to prevent current flowing.
A few minutes later, these measurements are repeated. How do the TWO sets of measurements compare?

With a half-life of only 30 seconds, ask what has happened to the number of undecayed Rh-106 nuclei after a few minutes, and then ask whether the energy released in each individual decay has changed.
A
The current is proportional to the rate at which electrons are emitted, which is proportional to the number of undecayed Rh-106 nuclei remaining:
With $T_{1/2} = 30\,\mathrm{s}$, several half-lives elapse in a few minutes, so a large fraction of the nuclei have decayed and the measured current $I$ has fallen substantially.

content.text: Explain what would be observed when the switch on cart 1 is closed. In your answer, refer to the current in each galvanometer and the initial movement of the carts.
Closing the switch is a momentary event. The flux through the solenoid on cart 2 changes for an instant and is then constant again, which matters for what galvanometer G2 shows afterwards.
Use Lenz's law to set the direction of the induced current in the solenoid on cart 2, then the magnetic pole that faces cart 1, and then the direction each cart is pushed.
Both carts are free to move, so once the directions are set, use conservation of momentum with the $2:1$ mass ratio to compare their final speeds.

When the switch is closed, a constant direct current will be observed on G1. This current will create a magnetic field in the solenoid with a south pole facing cart 2. As this field is generated, the solenoid on cart 2 experiences a momentary change in magnetic flux, inducing an emf and a current in the solenoid. By Lenz's law the direction of this current opposes the original change in flux, forming a south pole facing cart 1 and causing a momentary deflection of G2 in the opposite direction to the current in G1. The equal and opposite magnetic repulsion of the south poles causes the carts to move away from each other. To conserve momentum, cart 1 will have half the initial velocity of cart 2 since its mass is double that of cart 2.

content.text: In experiment B, the light is incident on different metal samples inside an evacuated tube as shown. The kinetic energy of any emitted photoelectrons can be measured.
Some results from experiment B are shown.
How do the results from Experiment A and Experiment B support TWO different models of light? In your answer, include a quantitative analysis of each experiment.
For experiment A, use $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ for the first order maxima. Because $\sin\theta$ is very small, the fringe spacing is approximately $y = L\sin\theta$.
For experiment B, calculate the energy of each photon from the wavelength of the source and compare that value with both of the work functions before deciding which metal emits.
Finish by naming the model of light that each result supports, and explain why the other experiment is not a contradiction: the two models describe different behaviour of the same light.

Experiment A: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{d} = \dfrac{400 \times 10^{-9}}{5.0 \times 10^{-5}} = 8.0 \times 10^{-3}$, so the fringe spacing on the screen is $y = L\tan\theta \approx 3.0 \times 8.0 \times 10^{-3} = 2.4 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}$, i.e. about 24 mm between adjacent bright (or dark) fringes. The pattern of bright and dark regions is explained by the wave model, where light from the two slits interferes constructively and destructively. Experiment B: the photon energy is $E = hf = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.00 \times 10^{8} \div 400 \times 10^{-9} = 4.97 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$. This exceeds the work function of calcium ($4.60 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$) but is less than that of nickel ($8.25 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$), explaining why photoelectrons are emitted from calcium only, and the maximum kinetic energy of the calcium photoelectrons is $K_{max} = 4.97 \times 10^{-19} - 4.60 \times 10^{-19} = 3.7 \times 10^{-20}\,\mathrm{J}$. This supports the particle (quantum) model of light, in which light consists of discrete photons of energy $hf$.

The pattern is explained by the wave model where light waves from the slits arrive at the screen causing bright regions at points of constructive interference and dark regions at points of destructive interference. This supports the wave model of light.

This energy is higher than the work function of calcium but not nickel, explaining why one photon has enough energy to liberate a photoelectron from the calcium sample, supporting the particle model of light.

content.text: Show that the energy released by one decay is $9.0 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$.
Write the mass balance for the decay: initial mass minus (final mass plus alpha particle mass) is the mass that has been converted into released energy.
That difference is very small, so subtract with enough decimal places kept; rounding the masses too early is the usual trap here.
Convert the mass deficit with $1\,\mathrm{u} = 1.66\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$ before applying $E = \Delta mc^{2}$, otherwise the result will be wrong by many orders of magnitude.
$E \approx 9.0 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$

items: 1 mark: sets up the correct relationship and substitutes the given values: $\Delta m = (238.0495 - 234.0409 - 4.0026)\,\mathrm{u} = 0.0060\,\mathrm{u} = 0.0060 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg} = 9.96 \times 10^{-30}\,\mathrm{kg}$
1 mark: correct intermediate working: $E = \Delta m c^{2} = 9.96 \times 10^{-30} \times (3.0 \times 10^{8})^{2} = 8.96 \times 10^{-13} \approx 9.0 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$
1 mark: correct final answer, $E \approx 9.0 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$, with correct units

content.text: At launch, the generator contains $9.0 \times 10^{24}$ atoms of Pu-238. The half-life of Pu-238 is 87.7 years.
Calculate the total energy produced by the generator during the first ten years after launch.
Turn the half-life into a decay constant with $\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}$, and keep the time in years so that it matches the ten-year interval and the units cancel.
The number of nuclei still present after time $t$ is $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$; the quantity you want is the difference $N_0 - N$, not $N_0$ itself.
Finally multiply the number of decays by the energy released in ONE decay, which you found in part (a).
$E \approx 6.2 \times 10^{11}\,\mathrm{J}$
